questions.q: Which three log sources does this project bring into Sentinel?
options: Windows Security Events, Linux Syslog, and the perimeter firewall
Only the perimeter firewall
Cloud storage logs, email logs, and DNS logs
Windows Security Events and nothing else
questions.explain: The plan covers Windows (already partially in place), Linux Syslog, and the perimeter firewall -- the two real blind spots plus confirming the existing coverage.

questions.q: What connector type do Windows Security Events and Linux Syslog both need?
options: Service-to-service
Agent-based, via the Azure Monitor Agent (AMA)
API-based
No connector is needed
questions.explain: Neither Windows servers nor Linux servers are Microsoft cloud services, so both need the Azure Monitor Agent installed to forward their logs.

questions.q: How does the perimeter firewall's log data actually reach Sentinel?
options: Directly, with no connector at all
Exported in CEF format to a Linux-based log forwarder running the AMA, which relays it into CommonSecurityLog
By manually copying log files into the workspace
Through the Windows Event Collector
questions.explain: The firewall exports CEF-formatted logs to an AMA-based forwarder, which relays the data into the CommonSecurityLog table.

questions.q: Which Sentinel table does firewall CEF data land in?
options: SecurityEvent
Syslog
CommonSecurityLog
SigninLogs
questions.explain: CEF-formatted logs, including from the perimeter firewall, land in CommonSecurityLog.

questions.q: Why does it matter to know the exact target table name before writing a correlation rule?
options: It doesn't matter at all
A rule that references the wrong table name simply returns nothing, with no error pointing at the mistake
Sentinel refuses to save a rule with an unknown table name
Table names change automatically based on query content
questions.explain: A query against the wrong (or a guessed) table name just returns an empty result -- it fails silently, which is why planning the tables first matters.
